Ovarian aging

PBM improved hormone, follicle, vascular, and mitochondrial measures in aged-mouse models. A 10-woman pilot found higher antral follicle counts but no statistically significant rise in retrieved oocytes. A separate controlled study found changes in ovarian-related gene expression after intravascular irradiation.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

PBM improved hormone, follicle, vascular, and mitochondrial measures in aged-mouse models. A 10-woman pilot found higher antral follicle counts but no statistically significant rise in retrieved oocytes. A separate controlled study found changes in ovarian-related gene expression after intravascular irradiation.

Summary of the Evidence

Three relevant publications were identified: one directly categorized study combining aged mice and cultured human granulosa cells, plus two narrowly mapped ovarian-aging studies. The human studies used different approaches and measured different outcomes. They are exploratory publications, not randomized trials of local ovarian PBM.

Human and clinical evidence

A non-randomized controlled study of 75 infertile women used intravascular laser blood irradiation and reported changes in cumulus-cell genes associated with oxidative-stress response and energy metabolism. These are laboratory markers, not evidence that ovarian reserve or fertility improved (Lin et al. 2024).

A 10-woman single-arm pilot of women with diminished ovarian reserve reported that median antral follicle count rose from 2 to 6 after daily red-light treatment before egg retrieval. The increase in retrieved oocytes was not statistically significant. Without a control group, the follicle-count change cannot by itself establish a treatment effect (Su et al. 2026).

Animal evidence

In naturally aged mice, 650-nm PBM at 4 J/cm² increased primordial and growing follicle counts, improved angiogenesis, reduced apoptosis and oxidative stress, and raised sex-hormone measures. A second study reported that daily 630-nm red light increased AMH, pregnancy rate, and litter size in aged mice, while 850-nm near-infrared light did not improve those outcomes. This direct wavelength contrast shows that the mouse results do not apply equally to all light protocols (He et al. 2024; Su et al. 2026).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

In hydrogen-peroxide-stressed KGN human granulosa cells, PBM increased viability, proliferation, hormone secretion, mitochondrial membrane potential, and ATP, while reducing apoptosis and oxidative-stress measures. These results concern a cell line under induced stress, not intact human ovaries (He et al. 2024).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The aged-mouse study used 650-nm red visible light at 4 J/cm², applied locally. The later mouse experiment compared 630-nm red light with 850-nm near-infrared light; in women, the wearable red-light device delivered 27 J/cm² for 30 minutes daily until retrieval. The intravascular study used 633-nm red light over 20 sessions. These routes and doses are not interchangeable, and no human dose-finding or head-to-head trial has been reported.

Interpretation

Animal experiments show improvements in several ovarian-function measures and a wavelength-specific reproductive result. In people, the strongest reported change is an uncontrolled increase in antral follicle count, while oocyte yield did not increase significantly and the other study measured gene expression. The findings justify clinical testing, but they do not yet establish improved pregnancy or live-birth rates in women.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for ovarian-function measures in aged-mouse models Very low for improved egg yield or live birth in women
Publications and records3 relevant articles (1 exact-category and 2 narrowly mapped)

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Two mouse studies report increases in follicle or hormone measures, and one of them also found better pregnancy and litter outcomes with red light but not near-infrared light. Human findings come from a small uncontrolled pilot and a non-randomized blood-irradiation study focused on biomarkers. Controlled trials measuring mature oocytes, pregnancy, and live birth are needed.
